title: Creating a Mini Herb‑Infused Salt for Grilling Steak at Home
meta_description: Elevate your BBQ with a homemade herb infused salt for grilling steak. Learn the best blends and how to prep fresh herbs quickly for a professional crust.
html:
There is a massive difference between a steak that is simply salted and one that features a complex, aromatic crust. While a basic kosher salt rub works, creating a custom herb infused salt grilling steak blend allows you to layer flavors—rosemary, thyme, and garlic—directly into the sear. The result is a steakhouse-quality crust that locks in juices and adds a sophisticated herbal note to every bite.

Choosing the Right Salt Base

The foundation of your infused salt determines how the herbs adhere to the meat. Avoid table salt; the grains are too fine and often contain anti-caking agents that can interfere with the flavor. Instead, reach for coarse Kosher salt or flaky sea salt.

Coarse grains create tiny pockets on the surface of the steak, allowing the minced herbs to nestle in rather than sliding off. This ensures that as the fat renders over the fire, the herbs toast in the oil, creating that savory, charred aroma we all crave.

The Secret to Perfectly Minced Herbs

The biggest mistake home cooks make with herb salts is leaving the pieces too large. If you have a whole rosemary needle or a large chunk of thyme sticking out, it will burn and turn bitter before the steak is actually cooked. You need a fine, consistent mince to ensure the flavor is distributed evenly across the cut.

This is where the right tool makes a difference. I personally use Herb Scissors to handle my prep. These five-blade herb shears allow you to mince cilantro, chives, and basil—or in this case, hardy grilling herbs—in one snip. It cuts the prep time down significantly and ensures the herbs are small enough to integrate perfectly with the salt crystals. Plus, the included cleaning comb makes it easy to clear out the sticky residue that usually gums up standard kitchen shears.

Best Herb Blends for Grilling Steak

Depending on the cut of meat, you may want to vary your aromatic profile. Here are three combinations that work exceptionally well for a herb infused salt grilling steak experience:

  • The Classic Steakhouse: Coarse salt, fresh rosemary, thyme, and a pinch of cracked black pepper. Ideal for Ribeyes and New York Strips.
  • The Mediterranean Twist: Coarse salt, flat-leaf parsley, dried oregano, and lemon zest. Perfect for Flank or Skirt steak.
  • The Garlic-Herb Punch: Coarse salt, fresh chives, parsley, and dehydrated garlic granules. Great for Filet Mignon.

How to Mix and Apply Your Herb Salt

To make the blend, place your coarse salt in a small bowl. Use your Herb Scissors to snip your fresh herbs directly into the salt. The multiple blades ensure the herbs are sliced thinly, which helps them release their essential oils more readily when they hit the heat.

For the best results, pat your steak completely dry with paper towels. Moisture is the enemy of a good sear. Apply the herb salt generously to all sides, pressing it firmly into the meat with your palms. Let the steak sit at room temperature for about 30 to 45 minutes before grilling. This gives the salt time to penetrate the meat and the herbs to adhere to the surface.

Grilling Tips for a Perfect Herb Crust

When using an herb infused salt grilling steak rub, temperature control is key. Because herbs can burn if the heat is too aggressive, start with a high-heat sear to lock in the juices, but move the steak to a medium-heat zone of the grill to finish cooking.

If you are using a cast-iron skillet on the grill, add a tablespoon of unsalted butter and a few extra sprigs of fresh thyme during the last two minutes of cooking. Spoon the foaming butter over the steak to amplify the herbal notes already present in your salt rub. Always let your steak rest for at least 10 minutes before slicing to ensure the juices redistribute.

FAQ

Can I make the herb salt in advance?

Yes, but for the best flavor, use dried herbs for long-term storage. If you use fresh herbs minced with Herb Scissors, use the salt within 24 hours, as the salt will draw moisture out of the fresh herbs, making the blend clump.

Will the herbs burn on the grill?

As long as the herbs are finely minced, they will toast rather than burn. Large pieces of herbs are more likely to char and become bitter, which is why a multi-blade shear is essential for a fine cut.

Which cut of steak works best with this method?

Thicker cuts like Ribeye or Filet Mignon are ideal because they stay on the grill longer, giving the herb salt more time to develop a rich, aromatic crust without overcooking the center.
